"HDI" redirects here. For other uses, see [HDI (disambiguation)](HDI_(disambiguation) "HDI (disambiguation)").

For the complete ranking of countries, see [List of countries by Human Development Index](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by Human Development Index").

The **Human Development Index** (**HDI**) is a statistical composite index of [life expectancy](Life_expectancy "Life expectancy"), [education](Education_Index "Education Index") (mean years of schooling completed and expected years of schooling upon entering the [education system](Educational_system "Educational system")), and [per capita income](Per_capita_income "Per capita income") indicators, which is used to rank countries into four tiers of [human development](Human_development_(humanity) "Human development (humanity)"). A country scores a higher level of HDI when the [lifespan](Life_expectancy_at_birth "Life expectancy at birth") is higher, the [education](Education "Education") level is higher, and the gross national income [GNI (PPP) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GNI_(PPP)_per_capita "List of countries by GNI (PPP) per capita") is higher. It was developed by Pakistani economist [Mahbub ul-Haq](Mahbub_ul_Haq "Mahbub ul Haq") and was further used to measure a country's development by the United Nations Development Programme (<UNDP>)'s Human Development Report Office.[[1]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-1)[[2]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-2)[[3]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-auto-3)

The 2010 [Human Development Report](Human_Development_Report "Human Development Report") introduced an [Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index](List_of_countries_by_inequality-adjusted_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by inequality-adjusted Human Development Index") (IHDI). While the simple HDI remains useful, it stated that "the IHDI is the actual level of human development (accounting for [inequality](Social_inequality "Social inequality")), while the HDI can be viewed as an index of 'potential' human development (or the maximum level of HDI) that could be achieved if there were no inequality."[[4]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-4)

The index is based on the human development approach, developed by [Mahbub ul-Haq](Mahbub_ul_Haq "Mahbub ul Haq"), anchored in [Amartya Sen's](Amartya_Sen "Amartya Sen") work on human capabilities, and often framed in terms of whether people are able to "be" and "do" desirable things in life. Examples include – being: well fed, sheltered, and healthy; doing: work, education, voting, participating in community life. The freedom of choice is central – someone choosing to be hungry (e.g. when [fasting](Fasting "Fasting") for religious reasons) is quite different from someone who is hungry because they cannot afford to buy food, or because the country is in a [famine](Famine "Famine").[[5]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-auto1-5)

The index does not take into account several factors, such as the [net wealth per capita](List_of_countries_by_wealth_per_adult "List of countries by wealth per adult") or the relative [quality of goods](Quality_(business) "Quality (business)") in a country. This situation tends to lower the ranking of some of the most [developed countries](Developed_countries "Developed countries"), such as the <G7> members and others.[[6]](Human_Development_Index#cite_note-6)

## Origins

The origins of the HDI are found in the annual Human Development Reports produced by the Human Development Report Office of the [United Nations Development Programme](United_Nations_Development_Programme "United Nations Development Programme") (UNDP). These were devised and launched by Pakistani economist [Mahbub ul-Haq](Mahbub_ul_Haq "Mahbub ul Haq") in 1990, and had the explicit purpose "to shift the focus of development economics from [national income](National_income "National income") accounting to [people-centered policies](People-centered_development "People-centered development")". Haq believed that a simple composite measure of human development was needed to convince the public, academics, and politicians that they can and should evaluate development not only by economic advances but also improvements in human [well-being](Well-being "Well-being").

- [Education](Education_index "Education index"): Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling

The [United Nations Development Programme](United_Nations_Development_Programme "United Nations Development Programme") (UNDP) compiles the [Human Development Index](Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") (HDI) of 191 nations in the annual [Human Development Report](Human_Development_Report "Human Development Report"). The index considers the [health](Health "Health"), [education](Education "Education"), [income](Income "Income") and living in a given country to provide a measure of [human development](Human_development_(economics) "Human development (economics)") which is comparable between countries and over time.[[1]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-overview-1)[[2]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-2022_components-2)

The HDI is the most widely used indicator of human development and has changed how people view the concept.[[3]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-3)[[4]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-quartz-4) However, several aspects of the index have received criticism. Some scholars have criticized how the factors are weighed, in particular how an additional year of life expectancy is valued differently between countries;[[4]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-quartz-4)[[5]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-5) and the limited factors it considers, noting the omission of factors such as the levels of distributional and gender inequality.[[6]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-6) In response to the former, the UNDP introduced the [inequality-adjusted Human Development Index](List_of_countries_by_inequality-adjusted_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by inequality-adjusted Human Development Index") (IHDI) in its 2010 report, and in response to the latter the [Gender Development Index](Gender_Development_Index "Gender Development Index") (GDI) was introduced in the 1995 report.[[7]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-7)[[8]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-8) Others have criticized the perceived oversimplification of using a single number per country.[[9]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-9)[[10]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-SHDI-10)

To reflect developmental differences within countries, a subnational HDI (SHDI) featuring data for more than 1,600 regions was introduced in 2018 by the Global Data Lab at [Radboud University](Radboud_University_Nijmegen "Radboud University Nijmegen") in the Netherlands.[[10]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-SHDI-10) In 2020, the UNDP introduced another index, the [planetary pressures–adjusted Human Development Index](List_of_countries_by_planetary_pressures%E2%80%93adjusted_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by planetary pressures–adjusted Human Development Index") (PHDI), which decreases the scores of countries with a higher ecological footprint.[[11]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-11)

## Dimensions and indicators

The HDI was first published in 1990 with the goal of being a more comprehensive measure of human development than purely economic measures such as [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product"). The index incorporates three dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and decent living standards. Various [indicators](Indicator_(statistics) "Indicator (statistics)") are used to quantify how countries perform on each dimension. The indicators used in the 2022 report were [life expectancy at birth](Life_expectancy "Life expectancy"); expected years of schooling for children; mean years of schooling for adults; and [gross national income](Gross_national_income "Gross national income") per capita. The indicators are used to create a health index, an education index and an income index, each with a value between 0 and 1. The [geometric mean](Geometric_mean "Geometric mean") of the three indices—that is, the cube root of the product of the indices—is the human development index. A value above 0.800 is classified as very high, between 0.700 and 0.799 as high, 0.550 to 0.699 as medium, and below 0.550 as low.[[1]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-overview-1)[[12]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-12)[[13]](List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index#cite_note-Technical_notes_2020-13)
